newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia shares mixed, low volume possible rise seen.
newsitem.headline: Russia shares mixed, low volume possible rise seen.

text.p: Russian shares ended mixed on Friday a day after President Boris Yeltsin's announcement that he would undergo heart surgery jolted the market, but traders said potential new investors would stay on the sideline.

Utility Mosenergo ticked up to $0.967 after Thursday's close of $0.960 and a pre-announcement trading range around $1.00. LUKoil closed up at $9.47 after $9.40 on Thursday and $9.84 on Thursday at 1314 GMT, about when news broke out.
UES fell to $0.0793 from $0.0795 and $0.0828 at the announcement. Surgutneftegaz fell to $0.382 from $0.405 and $0.419.
The Russian Trading System Index closed down 4.16 percent at 175.23 on relatively strong volume of $19.5 million.

"The aggressive money is already in and did not sell," said one Western fund manager. "The majority of people will be on the sidelines as prices go up on extremely thin volumes," until the operation, he predicted.

Trinfiko's Alexander Fonarkov also said Western investors, the driving force in the Russian market, would wait until the results of the heart bypass operation, which Yeltsin said would be at the end of the month, were clear.
"It is going to be a sideways market," Fonarkov said.

The fund manager said new money, especially large Western funds long expected to invest but waiting for stability, first from the July presidential election and now from Yeltsin's health, would come in waves as the future cleared.
But he said funds would wait to see Yeltsin firmly re-established as the country's leader -- not simply healthy in a hospital bed.
Traders had mixed predictions whether thin trade would rise or fall as the operation approached.

Western traders said domestic traders led a Friday morning low-volume sell-off which saw bid prices fall over 10 percent on Thursday afternoon levels, but when Western investors grabbed cheap shares the fall began to reverse itself.

"Local traders made a bet that the West was going to sell with a vengeance and that didn't happen," said Terry Olin of Troika-Dialog, who predicted the market would begin to slowly rise, as it has in recent weeks.
